issues.issue: The $100,000 accounts receivable limit stated here is increased to $1,000,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 1, so the policy carries two different figures for the same sublimit.

"Any loss that requires an audit or inventory to establish its existence" is undefined and could exclude nearly every accounts-receivable claim, since proof of receivables almost always involves accounting records.
"All reasonable efforts, including legal action if necessary" gives no benchmark for how much collection effort is required before the insured may claim.
Payment is the average monthly balance "adjusted for normal fluctuations ... or for any demonstrated variance," terms that supply no measurable standard for the adjustment.

"Fires of a suspicious nature" is a vague trigger, and the reward conditions are drafted so that payment depends on a third party's conviction or confession rather than on anything the insured controls.

The clause promises to pay "up to $25,000" but is written in exclusionary form ("caused by or resulting directly or indirectly from ... regardless of any other cause"), so whether it grants or restricts coverage is genuinely unclear.
"Immediate written notice" is a condition of payment with no defined period, leaving the point at which notice becomes untimely open to argument.
The $250,000 debris removal sublimit stated here is increased to $1,000,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 4.A, so two figures appear for the same sublimit.

This $25,000 windblown-debris figure is deleted and replaced by $50,000 in the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 4.B, so the policy states the same sublimit twice at different amounts.
"All reasonable effort, including legal action against your client" states no measure of what effort suffices before the insurer must pay.

The duty to defend is limited to "that part of any suit" meeting four conditions, yet the insurer reserves the right to settle "as we deem appropriate"; the interaction of a partial defense duty with unilateral settlement discretion is open to competing readings.
The sixty-day extended period stated here is amended to ninety days by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 7, so the policy states two different periods.

The breakage exclusion runs to "art glass windows, statuary, marble, glassware, bric-a-brac, porcelains, and similar fragile articles," and the reach of that general catch-all beyond the enumerated items is uncertain.

This extension pays fungus cleanup "up to the applicable limit of liability" while GROUP A exclusion 4 excludes fungus outright except where a specified peril ensues; which controls a fungus claim following fire is left to be harmonised.

The STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 10 recites that this $250,000 sublimit is "increased ... to $Not Applicable," leaving the operative figure contestable even though the item's box is unchecked.
"Immediate written notice" is an undefined condition precedent, with no stated period against which timeliness can be measured.
The promise to pay pollutant removal "subject to the applicable limit of liability" identifies no sublimit at all, in contrast with the express $25,000 aggregates in the two following subparagraphs.
This $25,000 annual aggregate is increased to $50,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 15.A, so the policy states the same aggregate twice at different amounts.
This $25,000 annual aggregate is increased to $50,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 15.B, leaving two different figures for the same coverage.
"Immediate written notice" fixes no period, so whether a given delay forfeits the pollution-cleanup expense is left open.
The $25,000 professional-fees sublimit here is increased to $50,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 16, so two figures appear for the same sublimit.
Coverage turns on property being at a location "under imminent threat by a peril insured against," a phrase with no temporal or probabilistic boundary.

The ninety-day temporary-location period stated here is deleted and replaced by "up to NA days" in the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 17, so the operative period is contradicted elsewhere.

The extension applies only where a loss is unpayable "solely because of" an error, then withdraws itself "if coverage is found, in whole or in part, elsewhere in this policy" — a self-cancelling pair of conditions whose combined effect is genuinely obscure.

It is difficult to reconcile with the Declarations Schedule condition that "insurance does not apply at locations ... unless a specific value is provided by you," which appears to defeat the very errors this extension is meant to cure.
This extension pays demolition cost while GROUP A exclusion 6 excludes "demolition cost, operation of building laws and increased cost of construction" without any stated exception for the extension.

The increased construction cost promised here is excluded outright by GROUP A exclusion 6 and is also carved out of the definition of "replacement cost," which excludes increased cost by reason of any law or ordinance.
Payment for rebuilding undamaged parts required by law sits against GROUP A exclusion 6, which excludes operation of building laws generally.
This says unscheduled locations "are insured," but the Declarations item E.4.k shows "$No Coverage" for unscheduled locations and E.1 provides that if no sublimit is shown no coverage is provided.

The anti-concurrent-causation preamble excludes loss "regardless of any other cause or event, including a peril insured against, that contributes to the loss," language whose effect on a mixed-cause loss is a recurring subject of construction.
